Chapter II - Protocol to Address Animal Cruelty Complaints

Inflicting unnecessary pain and suffering upon animals and subjecting them to cruelty is a criminal offense. Accordingly, all complaints of animal cruelty must be addressed in accordance with provisions of the following statutes –

Further, complaints pertaining to animal cruelty should be addressed in accordance with the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals Act, 1960 [“PCA, 1960”], and The Prevention of Cruelty to Animals (Care and Maintenance of Case Property Animals) Rules, 2017 [“Case Property Rules, 2017”].
The protocol to employed to address animal cruelty complaints is as below:
A. Upon Receipt of a Complaint:
Depending upon the nature of the offense, i.e., whether it is cognizable or non-cognizable;
the first step is to either register an First Information Report [“FIR”] - for cognizable offenses, or file a Non-Cognizable Report [“NCR”] - for non-cognizable offenses, as described below.

If details pertaining to the commission of cognizable offences are brought to the knowledge of a police officer in charge of the jurisdictional police station, the officer should register an FIR under Section 173 of BNSS, 2023.

II) In the matter of Lalita Kumari v. Government of Uttar Pradesh and Ors, [2014 (2) SCC 1], the Hon’ble Supreme Court directed that registration of an FIR is mandatory if the information discloses the commission of a cognizable offense.

III) The concept of Zero FIR has been explicitly mentioned in the BNSS, 2023 and is provided under Section 173 of BNSS, 2023. This Section also provides for registration of an FIR electronically (e-FIR).
IV) Section 173 of BNSS, 2023 requires that a copy of the FIR registered be provided to the victim along with the informant.

Further, as per Section 173 of BNSS, 2023, for cognizable offences which are punishable with sentence of 3 years or more but less than 7 years, the officer in charge of the police station may with the prior permission of the Deputy Superintendent of Police, conduct preliminary enquiry to ascertain whether there exists a prima facie case for proceeding in the matter within a period of 14 days and with the investigation when there exists a prima facie case.

VI) As per Section 168 BNSS, 2023, it is the duty of every police officer to prevent the commission of cognizable offenses, to the best of their ability. This entails informing superior officers of the police, in accordance with Section 169 of BNSS, 2023. Section 170 of BNSS, 2023 also provides for arresting suspects if the situation requires.

If details pertaining to the commission of non-cognizable offenses are brought to the knowledge of a police officer in charge of the jurisdictional police station, the concerned officer should ensure that the details of the offense are recorded as entries in a register, as per 174(1) of BNSS, 2023.
II) The concerned officer is also required to refer such information to the Magistrate.
Section 174(1) of BNSS, 2023 also requires that the Daily Diary report of all such cases shall be forwarded on a fortnightly basis to the Magistrate.
A3) Examination of Complainant by Magistrate:
Section 223 read with Section 225 of BNSS, 2023 states that the Magistrate can take cognizance of an offence without the knowledge of the accused person.

II) Further, Section 223 of BNSS, 2023 has introduced another aspect which states that the Magistrate shall afford the accused an opportunity to be heard before the Court proceeds to take cognizance of an offence based on the complaint.
B1) Requirement of Orders from the Magistrate Prior to Investigation of Offenses:
Cognizable offenses can be investigated without orders from a Magistrate, as per Section 175(1) of BNSS, 2023.

II) Any Magistrate empowered under Section 210 of BNSS, 2023 may order an investigation of any cognizable offence as per Section 175 (3) of BNSS, 2023. Further, as per Section 175 (3) of BNSS, 2023 the Magistrate may order for an investigation on private complaints upon-
Making an enquiry on a complaint made by the complainant
Considering the submissions made by the police officer regarding the complaint made

III) Section 175 (4) of BNSS, 2023 further deals with complaints against public officials, where the Magistrate is empowered under Section 210 of BNSS, 2023, and can order investigation against public official subject to-
Receiving a report containing facts and circumstances of the incident from the officer superior to the concerned public servant
After consideration of the assertions made by the public servant, as to the situation that leads to the incident so alleged
IV) The police are required to obtain orders from a Magistrate prior to investigating noncognizable offenses, as per Section 174(2) of BNSS, 2023.

Upon appropriate directions from the Magistrate in this regard, the investigation of non-cognizable offenses can proceed, following the same course as investigation for cognizable offenses. The same is detailed in Section 174(3) of BNSS, 2023.
B2) Copy of Report for Cognizable Offences to be Sent to the Magistrate

In case of cognizable offenses, the Magistrate must be kept apprised on the status of the investigation as detailed in Section 176(1) of BNSS, 2023, by providing a copy of the report pertaining to the offenses.
B3) Records to be Maintained by the Investigating Officer
The Investigating Officer [“IO”] assigned to the case is responsible for maintaining records of the investigation in a case diary, as required in Section 192 of BNSS, 2023.
II) The IO should ensure details pertaining to the statements recorded, findings arrived at through investigation and other key aspects are duly recorded.
B4) Powers of the Police While Conducting Investigations
The powers of police officers carrying out investigations draw from provisions of the BNSS, PCA, 1960 and the Case Property Rules, 2017, as detailed below -

As per Section 179 of BNSS, 2023 the police officer conducting the investigation has the power to require attendance of witnesses. The officer can through written communication, seek attendance of persons who appear to be acquainted with the facts and circumstances of the case. The persons the police officer may call upon for attendance, must belong to either the jurisdiction of the said officer’s police station or the jurisdiction of the adjoining ones.

II) Section 180 of BNSS, 2023 also provides for the police officers carrying out the investigation to orally examine witnesses. The recording of statements pursuant to such examination is also provided for.

III) Officers are also empowered to carry out searches while investigating the commission of offenses, as per Section 185 of BNSS, 2023. Further, as per Section 185 of BNSS, 2023, the search conducted shall be recorded through audio-video electronic means, preferably by mobile phones. Section 185 of BNSS, 2023 should be read in consonance with Section 105 of BNSS, 2023.

IV) In terms of Sections 32 and 34 of PCA, 1960, police officers holding the rank of Sub- Inspector [“SI”] or above, are empowered to carry out search and seizure while investigating offenses under PCA, 1960.

Section 33 of PCA, 1960 provides for the circumstance when the Commissioner of Police/District Superintendent of Police has reason to believe offenses under this Act are being, are about to be, or have been committed in any place. In such a scenario, they may either themselves enter and search or authorize any police officer of the rank of SI or above to carry out such entry and search at the concerned premises.
B5) Seizure of Animals by the Police

Upon having reason to believe an offense under PCA, 1960 has been committed, any police officer holding a rank of a constable or above, is empowered under Section 34 of PCA, 1960 to seize an animal against whom the said offense is believed to have been committed. This Section provides similar seizing power to the constable for offenses that are being or are about to be committed.
II) The Constable is required to produce the seized animal for examination before the jurisdictional veterinary officer [“JVO”], as provided for in Section 34 of PCA, 1960.
III) In accordance with Rule 3 of the Case Property Rules, 2017, the police shall ensure the health inspection, identification, and marking of the animal through the JVO.
Subsequently, the seized animal, who is treated as case property, is to be produced before the Magistrate.

Articles believed to have been used in offenses against animals and which may thus hold evidentiary value, are to be taken into custody of the police as per Section 106 of BNSS, 2023. The articles are to be presented before the Magistrate accompanied by photographic documentation, health and forensic reports. Such articles include weapons like knives/sticks, heavy chains, cages/receptacles and so forth.
II) As per Section 63 of BSA, 2023, videos, CCTV footage, photographs and other electronic records are considered as electronic evidence.

III) In the scenario that the electronic evidence cannot be produced in court, recourse may be taken to Section 63(4) of BSA, 2023. A certificate of attestation for the evidence, the recording device and the circumstances of such recording can be referred to. The said certificate must be duly signed by the person who operates the device as well.
IV) Rule 5(4) of the Case Property Rules, 2017 provides for any vehicle(s) used in commission of offenses under PCA, 1960 being seized and subsequently produced before the Magistrate.
C. Specific Protocols for Animals Seized by the Police:
Depending upon whether the animals against whom the offenses have been carried out are
alive, deceased or mortally wounded/diseased, the specific protocols may vary as below
C1) If the Animal is Alive
While conducting a search in a case of animal cruelty, if the police officer finds the animal is alive, the protocol is to seize the animal, as per Section 34 of PCA, 1960.

II) The next course of action as per Rule 3 of the Case Property Rules, 2017, is for the police officer to contact the JVO for identification tagging and health examination of the animal, as per the manner prescribed.
III) If it is found that the animal has sustained injuries/is suffering illness, they must be provided the necessary medical treatment as per Section 35 of PCA, 1960.

IV) Subsequently, the animal is to be produced before the Magistrate. The Magistrate has the power to decide upon the custody of the animal pending litigation as per Rule 3 of the Case Property Rules, 2017.

As per Rule 5 of the Case Property Rules, 2017, the cost of care and maintenance of the animals is to be borne by the accused. The accused is required to furnish bonds within 3 days, failing which the animal will be deemed to be forfeited.

VI) The seized animal is to be housed at the premises of the infirmary/pinjrapole/SPCA/Animal Welfare Organisation that has been granted custody by the Magistrate as per Rules 3-5 of the Case Property Rules, 2017.
C2) If the Animal is Deceased

If the police officer finds that the animal against whom offenses have been/are alleged to have been committed is deceased, the officer shall contact the JVO to carry out a Post-Mortem Examination of the animal.
II) The police officer must ensure prompt seizure of the body of the animal and handover the same to the JVO for expeditiously carrying out the Post-Mortem Examination.
III) The report arising from the Post-Mortem Examination which details the cause of death of the animal should accompany the investigation report as well as find reflection in the case diary.
C3) If the Animal is Mortally Wounded/Diseased
Upon coming across animals suffering severe injury/disease, a police officer above the rank of constable has the authority to contact the JVO and seek medical examination of the animal.

II) If the JVO is of the opinion that the animal is incurably injured/ill, and keeping the animal alive would prolong unnecessary pain and suffering - euthanasia may be carried out. All cases of euthanasia would require the JVO certifying the need for the same and obtaining consent from the Magistrate as per Section 13 of PCA, 1960.
D. Protocol for Cases where Injurious Substances are Found:
D1) The protocol to be followed upon finding injurious substances (including drugs)
used in offenses committed/alleged to have been against animals is similar to that followed in general cases involving illegal drugs.
D2) The injurious substances are required to be seized and sent to the designated laboratory.
D3) If a Drug Inspector is present at the site and part of the search team, the seized substances must be sealed by the Drug Inspector and sent to the designated laboratory.

Judgement of the Hon’ble Supreme Court dated 12.11.2013 in Lalita Kumari v.s Government of Uttar Pradesh and Ors [2014 (2) SCC 1]: The Hon’ble Supreme Court directed that registration of an FIR is mandatory if the information discloses the commission of a cognizable offence and no preliminary enquiry is permissible in all cases where a cognizable offence is made out. The only scenario where preliminary inquiry is permissible is when there is a need to verify the nature of information received (in terms of the offence being cognizable or not). The Apex Court directed that the scope of the preliminary inquiry cannot be expanded to verify the veracity of the complaint, prior to registration of an FIR.
2. Order of the Hon’ble Supreme Court dated 05.02.2020 in Raghuramsharma &

Anr. v.s C. Thulsi & Anr. [Crl. A. 230/2022]: The Hon'ble Supreme Court of India in this case directed that the interim custody of the cattle should not be handed over to the accused. It was further directed that custody of the cattle/animals be retained by the appellants, subject to verification of their profile and the identity of the cattle. These directives illustrate the importance of ensuring animals who have been prima facie subject to cruelty are not returned to the accused.
Order of the Hon’ble Supreme Court dated 26.09.2022 in Meher Banu Begum v.

State of Assam & Anr. [Misc. Application No. 1620/2022 in SLP(Crl) No. 9997/ 2021]: The Apex Court of India affirmed that failure to pay the bond as required under Rule 5 of the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals (Care and Maintenance of Case Property Animals) Rules, 2017 can result in the forfeiture of the animal. This underscores the principle that the Case Property Rules, 2017 do not allow the return of the animal's custody to the accused.
Chapter III - Broad Legal Framework for Offences Involving Animals

The legal frameworks provided by the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals Act, 1960 [“PCA, 1960”], and Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 [“BNS, 2023”] are instrumental in safeguarding animal welfare in India. PCA, 1960 is a welfare legislation, enacted to prevent and alleviate the unnecessary pain and suffering of animals. This Act defines various offences and stipulates corresponding penalties. Additionally, BNS, 2023 contains provisions pertaining to acts of mischief towards animals, entailing cruelty as well as acts that involve animals and endanger public health and safety.

Within this legislation, there are provisions pertaining to public health and safety as well as animal cruelty. Chapter V - Provisions Pertaining to Animal Birth Control and Community Animals

In the face of human-dog conflict, several attempts at exterminating community dogs in India have been undertaken. These have yielded abysmal results - both in terms of their failure to control dog populations as well as in reducing rabies incidence or human-dog conflict. The Animal Birth Control Rules, 2023 [“ABC Rules, 2023”], provide for an ethical, humane and efficient solution to address the aforementioned issues. The ABC Rules, 2023 should be read in conjunction with Sections 11(1) and 38 of the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals Act, 1960 [“PCA,1960”] and the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 [“BNS, 2023”].
